prompt: Write an email to a colleague about rumors going around town. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Re: What's going around town

Hi Jordan,

I hope your week is going well. I wanted to reach out before the rumor mill gets any further ahead of the facts, because I've heard a few things around town lately and figured you probably have too.

The main one making the rounds is that the Harbor Street office is closing by the end of the year. I've heard it from three different people now, each with a slightly different version. One says the whole building is being sold, another says only our floor is affected, and a third insists the company is moving everyone to the new campus across the river. None of them can point to an actual source, which makes me think this is mostly speculation that keeps getting repeated until it sounds official.

There's also talk that leadership is planning a restructuring in January. I'll be honest, that one worries me a bit more, since it's the kind of thing that can really rattle a team. A couple of people in accounting mentioned they'd seen unusual meetings on the executive calendar, but meetings alone don't tell us much. Executives meet all the time, and not every closed-door conversation means layoffs.

Finally, someone told me the hiring freeze is being extended through spring. That one at least seems plausible, given how the last quarter went, but I haven't seen anything in writing.

Here's where I land. I don't think any of us should treat these stories as fact, and I'd rather we not add fuel by passing them along. When people are anxious, even a casual "I heard that..." can spread fast and turn into something much bigger. I'd suggest we keep an eye on the official announcements and, if things stay unclear, ask our manager directly at the next team meeting. A straightforward question usually gets a more reliable answer than anything we'll pick up in the break room.

That said, I don't want to dismiss your concerns if you've heard something different. If you have any firsthand information, or if someone in your department has been given a heads-up about changes, I'd really like to know. It's helpful to compare notes, as long as we're careful to separate what we actually know from what we've only heard.

Would you be free for coffee on Thursday afternoon? We could talk it through in person, and I'd like to hear what your team has been saying. Let me know what works for you.

Take care, and try not to let the gossip get to you.

Best,
[name]
